subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me a challenging KS3 geography question on {lo}, then mark my answer.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for KS3 simply, with an example and the most common mistake.
learningObjectives: Choose maps, atlases, globes and GIS to locate places and features

questions.lo: Choose maps, atlases, globes and GIS to locate places and features
questions.q: You want to view your local town, switch on a layer showing flood risk, and measure a distance on screen. Which tool is designed for this?
questions.explain: GIS (Geographical Information Systems) let you zoom in, turn data layers on and off, and measure digitally. A globe or paper atlas cannot layer or measure data in this way.

questions.lo: Choose maps, atlases, globes and GIS to locate places and features
questions.q: Which tool shows the true shape and size of the continents most accurately?
questions.explain: A globe is 3D so it shows the Earth without distortion. Every flat map has to stretch or squash something, so shapes and sizes are slightly wrong.

questions.lo: Read and give 4-figure and 6-figure grid references (eastings before northings)
questions.q: When giving a grid reference, which number do you always read first?
questions.explain: Eastings come before northings: read along the bottom first, then up the side. A handy memory aid is 'along the corridor, then up the stairs'.

questions.lo: Read and give 4-figure and 6-figure grid references (eastings before northings)
questions.q: What does a 4-figure grid reference identify on an OS map?
questions.explain: A 4-figure reference names a whole square using its bottom-left corner. To pinpoint an exact spot you need a 6-figure reference, which splits the square into tenths.

questions.lo: Read and give 4-figure and 6-figure grid references (eastings before northings)
questions.q: A feature sits in the square whose bottom-left corner is where easting 21 meets northing 47. What is its 4-figure grid reference?
questions.explain: Easting first (21), then northing (47), giving 2147. Reversing them to 4721 is the most common mistake.

questions.lo: Read and give 4-figure and 6-figure grid references (eastings before northings)
questions.q: How many digits are in a 6-figure grid reference, and what extra precision does it give?
options: Four digits; it names a square
Six digits; each square is split into tenths for an exact point
Two digits; it gives a direction
Eight digits; it gives a height
questions.explain: A 6-figure reference has six digits. Each grid square is imagined as a 10x10 grid, so the extra digits pinpoint an exact point rather than just a square.

questions.lo: Use compass points and direction
questions.q: Which compass point lies exactly between north and east?
questions.explain: North-east (NE) sits halfway between N and E on the 8-point compass. The eight points, clockwise, are N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW.

questions.lo: Use compass points and direction
questions.q: A bearing is measured clockwise from north. Which bearing points due west?
questions.explain: North is 000, east is 090, south is 180 and west is 270 degrees, measured clockwise. A full turn back to north is 360 degrees.

questions.lo: Use scale to convert map distance to real distance
questions.q: On a 1:25 000 map, what real distance does 1 cm on the map represent?
questions.explain: 1:25 000 means 1 cm on the map equals 25 000 cm on the ground. 25 000 cm = 250 m (or 0.25 km).

questions.lo: Use scale to convert map distance to real distance
questions.q: On a 1:25 000 map (1 cm = 250 m), a footpath measures 4 cm. How long is the real path?
questions.explain: Real distance = map distance x scale: 4 cm x 250 m = 1000 m (1 km).

questions.lo: Use scale to convert map distance to real distance
questions.q: On a 1:50 000 map, 1 cm = 500 m. A road measures 6 cm on the map. How far is that in real life?
questions.explain: 6 cm x 500 m = 3000 m, which is 3 km. Converting metres to kilometres by dividing by 1000 is a key step.

questions.lo: Interpret contour lines and relief
questions.q: What do contour lines on an OS map join together?
questions.explain: Contour lines join points that are the same height above sea level. The number on each line tells you that height.

questions.lo: Interpret contour lines and relief
questions.q: A hillside shows contour lines drawn very close together. What does this tell you?
questions.explain: Closely-spaced contours mean the height changes over a short distance, so the slope is steep. Spacing shows steepness, not the actual height.

questions.lo: Interpret contour lines and relief
questions.q: Two slopes are shown. Slope A has widely-spaced contours; slope B has tightly-packed contours. Which is the gentler slope?
questions.explain: Widely-spaced contour lines mean the height rises gradually over a long distance, so slope A is the gentler one. Tightly-packed lines (slope B) mean steep ground.

questions.lo: Interpret Ordnance Survey map symbols and keys
questions.q: You see an unfamiliar symbol on an OS map. What is the best way to find out what it means?
options: Look it up in the map's key
questions.explain: The key (legend) printed on the map explains every symbol. You do not need to memorise them all, you look them up.

questions.lo: Interpret Ordnance Survey map symbols and keys
questions.q: A tourist wants a place to pitch a tent. Which OS symbol should they look for in the key?
questions.explain: An open triangle is the campsite symbol. A blue P means parking, and the tower symbol marks a church.

questions.lo: Interpret OS maps alongside aerial and satellite photographs
questions.q: You need the exact height of a hill and a grid reference for its summit. Which source gives you this?
questions.explain: Only an OS map carries contour heights, spot heights and a grid, so you can read exact height and give a grid reference. A photo shows appearance but no measurements.

questions.lo: Carry out fieldwork to observe, measure, record and present data
questions.q: You count cars at a junction yourself during a fieldtrip. What type of data is this?
questions.explain: Data you collect yourself in the field is primary data. Data taken from a book, website or someone else is secondary data.

questions.lo: Carry out fieldwork to observe, measure, record and present data
questions.q: You measured river temperature every hour through the day and want to show how it changed over time. Which is the best way to present it?
questions.explain: A line graph is best for showing continuous change over time. A bar chart suits separate categories and a pie chart shows proportions of a whole.

questions.lo: Carry out fieldwork to observe, measure, record and present data
questions.q: In a traffic survey you counted 10, 14 and 12 cars in three time slots. What is the mean number of cars per slot?
questions.explain: Add the values (10 + 14 + 12 = 36) then divide by how many there are (3): 36 / 3 = 12.
